11200-the-world-war-and-what-was-behind-:
L. P. Bénézet, superintendent of schools in Evansville, Indiana, wrote this history for young readers to explain the First World War through the map of Europe. Starting with Rome and the barbarian tribes, he traces chiefs becoming kings, the rise of modern nations, and the making of a king-made map full of wrongs. Chapters on Bismarck, the balance of power, and the Entente Cordiale lead to the spark that exploded the magazine.

Maps and a pronouncing glossary support the text, and later chapters ask who profited, why England and the United States entered, and what Europe should become. The book's argument is moral as well as historical: wars grow from unjust borders. As a school text of its era, it shows how American classrooms first framed the Great War.
11584-madcap:
George Gibbs opens Madcap with Hermia, whose maid Titine finds her bed empty before eight in the morning. Miss Challoner has gone for a cold ride on a violent horse after a late night out.

Chapters follow through a gorilla, an ineffectual aunt, a marooning, bread and salt, and a rescue. Olga Tcherny, the Fabiani family, danger, and a philosopher in a quandary keep the plot moving. Later scenes bring a lady in the dark, the wings of a butterfly, and a brass bell. The book is a light romance of adventure, flirtation, and narrow escapes.
14376-somewhere-in-red-gap:
Harry Leon Wilson wrote this Red Gap book, a set of linked tales round Ma Pettengill and her ranch folk. The narrator's living room opens the first tale, where romance splashes red across plain life. Ma Pettengill returns, sharp-tongued and warm, with Cousin Egbert, Kate, and Pete's kin in tow. Wilson tells the tales in his first-person voice.

One tale gives Angus and Ellabelle a child, with a chest already broad as a clock shelf, and a fight over naming a son. Another shows a gate with hinges, cords, and an open and shut, which Ma calls a per-diem gate. The narrator means the rite as a lesson to his hostess, and she answers in kind. The book charms as a string of ranch yarns, where wit, pride, and affection mix. Its humor stays even when the folk are at odds.
14600-theory-of-silk-weaving-a-treatise-:
Arnold Wolfensberger, graduate of the Textile Institute of Zurich, wrote this treatise on silk weaving, in a second revised edition issued in New York in 1921 by the American Silk Journal. Ninety-five plates illustrate the text.

The book explains drawing-in, the order of warp threads through heddles, and the construction of taffeta, cannelé, and Jacquard weaves, with designs showing face and back. Wolfensberger treats broad and narrow, plain and novelty fabrics in technical detail. The treatise served weavers, designers, and mills, and it remains a reference for textile history.
16586-the-voyage-of-the-rattletrap:
Hayden Carruth's 1897 travel tale follows a prairie schooner called the Rattletrap. It runs from Lookout Lake to the Missouri, across Nebraska and the Niobrara, through sand hills and antelope flats, to the Black Hills and Deadwood, then homeward bound. Grandpa Oldberry presages disaster, a pony mutinies, and a heifer wears a sleigh robe along the way.

Carruth writes with humor and a pioneer's eye for camp life, hay twisting, and grouse shooting. The book is dedicated to John Briar, a poor cook but a good fellow. Readers of western travel will enjoy a light, lively wagon journey across the plains.
17056-the-submarine-boys-and-the-middies:
Victor G. Durham wrote this 1909 third book of eight in the Submarine Boys series, The Prize Detail at Annapolis. Chapters move from the prize detail and Eph flirting with science into a bridge order and a guess from Mr. Farnum. Truax sulking, two kinds of voodoo, and Jack finding something new follow. A young captain in tatters, a squint at a camel, and a sea cruise appear. The Pollard going lame, hard luck, and marines lead to a verdict and no more men overboard.

Durham sends Jack Benson and his mates to Annapolis, where middies, marines, and submarine trials test their nerve. The tale mixes academy life with undersea adventure. Young readers get a brisk, old-style boys' book, full of pranks, peril, and a prize detail that rewards courage and quick thinking.
19547-obed-hussey-who-of-all-inventors-m:
Follett L. Greeno edited this life of Obed Hussey, the inventor whose reaper helped make bread cheap, published in the early nineteen teens. Gathered from pamphlets by Hussey's friends, it follows his struggle to introduce the machine and win it success.

Hussey, of Quaker stock born in Maine, once dreamed of whaling voyages before turning to farm tools. A dispute over the raker's seat, used by Hussey years before rivals patented it, shows how invention honors were fought. The book is a plain record of a working inventor. One passage reports English trials where Hussey's machine cut corn with neatness and certainty.
21318-the-lost-middy-being-the-secret-of:
Aleck, a sixteen-year-old orphan, lives by the sea with an uncle whose whole interest is writing a history book. Aleck sails his little boat along the coast with Tom Bodger, a pensioned man-of-war's man. George Manville Fenn then brings a press gang raid to their shore, backed by a revenue cutter.

Local men are seized for the navy. But the smugglers of the hamlet seize a prize of their own: a midshipman from the sloop, hidden in the smugglers' own cave. Aleck stumbles onto their track and is shut in the same cave, both mouths blocked. Fenn leaves his two prisoners in the dark to work the title's secret out.
23195-wikkey-a-scrap:
Wikkey, signed by Yam, tells the story of a young street sweeper. Wikkey is first seen holding his broom beneath a lamp-post where his crossing ends. There he first set eyes on Lawrence Granby, the man on whom the whole tale turns.

The narrator is blunt about that link: had Wikkey never seen Granby, there would be no story to write. Giving the boy another trade, he adds, would not mend matters much. Readers get a Victorian city tale built on one chance meeting between a poor crossing sweeper and a man from a very different world.
24151-the-sky-trap:
Frank Belknap Long wrote this science fiction story of a future Earth that has tamed its own violence. Lawton, a weather man on a stratoship high above the world, starts his day by trading blows with Slashaway Tommy, a lean gym slugger, on the ship's tilted athletic deck. In this age, men work off their fighting urge in the gym, eight or ten times a week, and world wars have ceased.

Lawton's weekly duty is to run weather instruments in the warm upper air for forty-five minutes, and his forecasts flash across Earth within minutes. Captain Forrester watches the bout with a reproachful eye. Readers get a sharp sketch of a managed future, where peace is kept by scheduled sport and science, and something in the sky waits to test it.
26799-narrative-of-the-captivity-of-will:
William Biggs wrote this captivity narrative himself, reprinted as number thirty-seven of Heartman's Historical Series, in eighty-one copies plus five on Japan paper. It tells his captivity among the Kickapoo Indians in Illinois in 1788.

On March 28, 1788, Biggs rode from Bellfontain to Cahokia with John Vallis of Maryland, when sixteen Indians rose with guns presented about forty yards away. Their single platoon volley put four bullets into his horse and four or five through his great coat. Biggs lost his gun, his saddle turned for want of girth and crupper, and he ran, feeling at every step the scalping knife on his scalp, until the Indians slacked their chase. A later night scene finds an Indian astride him, rubbing a tomahawk across his forehead and threatening death for wanting to run away.
29546-where-half-the-world-is-waking-up-:
Clarence Poe's book on Japan, copyrighted in 1911, takes its title from a waking world: where half the world is waking up, the old and the new in Japan. A frontispiece shows Count Shige-Nobu Okuma, among the Genro, the elder statesmen of Japan, and a former premier, given from a photograph and autograph to the author. Poe thanks fellow travelers, among them Adams of Akron, Ohio, and Dr. Arthur Mez of Mannheim, for the use of many photographs.

Poe writes of a Japan balancing tradition and change, with American conditions as his point of comparison. The book mixes travel, portrait, and reflection on a nation remaking itself. Readers of Japan and of Progressive-era travel writing will find a vivid, optimistic account of an empire in transition.
31094-bear-trap:
Alan E. Nourse wrote this science fiction story, by the author of many mystery and science fiction stories including Martyr, the lead novel in a January 1957 issue. 

A huge troop transport plane eases down through rainy drizzle at New York International Airport at about five in the evening. Tom Shandor glances sourly through the port at the rainy wet landing strip, with dim landing lights reflected in steaming puddles. Rows of jet fighters stand on an adjacent field, wings up in the dark foggy rain, poised like ridiculous birds. He rips a sheet of paper from a small, battered portable typewriter, checks the date, September 27, 1982, and rolls the sheets for mailing. It is a tense, futuristic tale.
31583-the-venus-trap:
Evelyn E. Smith's science-fiction story The Venus Trap, illustrated by Dick Francis, was produced from Galaxy Science Fiction of June 1956. It opens with James asking Phyllis anxiously whether she likes the planet. Phyllis loves it, she says. Blue grass and blue-violet shrubs please her, and most of all a tall golden tree with sapphire leaves and pink blossoms, which makes the place feel like a fairy-tale Earth. Even the fragrance is delightful to terrestrial nostrils, which is unusual, since most planets, from the human viewpoint, tend to stink.

Smith's trap, as the title warns, lies in that very beauty. A planet too perfect for colonists, with an eternal triangle waiting in its garden, makes for comedy and danger at once. Readers will find a witty, romantic science-fiction story, where love and colonization meet on a world designed to please.
32718-the-trap:
Betsy Curtis tells of old Miss Barbara Noble, who watches her street from a second-floor sitting room. A young salesman with a battered black case climbs her porch and rings her bell, and Barbara studies his limp hair and stained shirt through a crack in the curtain. She pities him, yet she will not let him in at once.

The salesman offers the wares of a future age, from face paint to devices that promise youth, and Barbara answers with her vizer screen and sharp tongue. She has made up her mind: no one will make her young again against her will. The tale is a wry stand for age on its own terms.
32913-through-south-africa-his-visit-to-:
Henry M. Stanley's Through South Africa gathers letters he wrote from Bulawayo, Johannesburg, and Pretoria for the journal South Africa, each letter summing a week's research. Stanley presents these as the fresh impressions of a first view of the South African interior. He had long been connected with equatorial, northern, and western Africa since 1867, and he had no political or money interest in the country.

Rather than repeat the history, geography, and politics that other books already covered, he records what he saw. The sights include towns, mines, peoples, and the feel of a region on the edge of great change. The letters are opinionated and personal, as travel writing of the period often was. They remain useful for the ground-level detail of Rhodesia and the Transvaal just before the century turned.
34247-caught-in-a-trap:
Caught in a Trap is a novel of society and sport that opens, in volume one, among the plungers, the heavy gamblers of London. Tom Hartshorne of the Dragoons walks into a private billiard room in Oxford Street one summer afternoon. There he finds his friend Markworth, tall, dark, and handsome, knocking the balls about in his shirt-sleeves.

Tom has come with a problem. He must spend his annual week at his mother's place in Sussex, a dreary house ruled by clockwork. Worse, the quiet visit threatens to bore him to death, and he wants rescue. Markworth, just back from Boulogne and at his friend's service, is the man to supply it. The scene sets a tale of money, pleasure, and the traps that wait for young men of fashion.
3792-capitola-the-madcap:
Emma Southworth continues her Hidden Hand saga in this sequel, with the madcap orphan Capitola at its center. Chapters carry Cap from an orphan's trial to the Hidden House and the Hidden Hollow, where she frees a captive, falls into captivity herself, and spars with the villain Black Donald. Old Hurricane storms, court martials, and a fatal hatred raise the stakes, while a mysterious maniac's story adds a second mystery.

A later scene shows Herbert watching recruits drill, struck by a familiar form in a private's uniform, a lost lover in disguise. Southworth writes at full melodramatic tilt, with disguises, rescues, and reversals on every page. Readers who like Victorian sensation fiction will find Capitola a heroine who never waits to be saved.
38544-life-of-luther-with-several-introd:
Life of Luther is a church history biography by Gustav Just, translated from the German. The Concordia Publishing House of St. Louis issued it in 1903. Chapters before the life itself cover the first Christians, the persecutions, and Constantine. Chapters on popery and monkery and the forerunners of the Reformation lead into Luther's childhood.

The life follows Luther through student days, the cloister, and his work as a teacher. It names him reformer, mighty warrior, and staunch confessor in turn. The Marburg meeting, the Augsburg Confession, and his Bible and hymnbook each get a chapter. The book ends with his family life and last days. It is a Lutheran life for church readers, plainly confessional in aim.
43040-consumers-and-wage-earners-the-eth:
Consumers and Wage-Earners is an economics treatise by Elliot Ross, printed at New York in 1912. Its subtitle states its theme: the ethics of buying cheap. A note says Ross came of an old Southern family and had long studied economics and sociology. The Catholic University gave him its doctorate for this very work.

The chapters state the point at issue, then the obligations of the consuming class. What is a just employer comes next, with a theory of industrial organization. Industrial conditions follow in wages, in health, and in morals. The book closes on what the individual consumer should do. Ross holds the shopper answerable for the sweated wage behind the bargain counter. It is Catholic social teaching aimed at the American housewife's basket.
45405-pickett-s-gap:
Homer Greene wrote Pickett's Gap, a novel printed in New York, rights held in 1902 and reprinted in 1904, with drawings first used in a youth magazine. Abner Pickett opens the tale, standing on his grandfather's land and vowing to stand where he pleases on it. A print shows him on a wall, gun in hand, ready for action.

Survey stakes in his ground are the spark: no better deed, says a voice, than to pull their accursed stakes and fling them in the brook. A contract signed, blame owned, and a door held open mark the turns. Young readers get a tale of land, pride, and right in the hills.
46449-the-manufacture-of-paper-with-illu:
Sindall wrote The Manufacture of Paper, a trade book for the paper industry. The catalog title is cut down to its last words, but the title page gives the full name. Sindall worked as a consulting chemist to the wood pulp and paper trades. He also lectured on paper making for a technical school in Hertfordshire.

His book explains how paper is made, from raw pulp to the finished sheet. It was written for men who worked in mills and for students of the trade. Pictures and a list of further reading support the text. Books like this one record the craft side of an industry most readers never think about, though they handle its product every day of their lives.
52286-the-colleges-of-oxford-their-histo:
Andrew Clark, a fellow of Lincoln College, edited this book of twenty-one chapters on the colleges of Oxford, printed by Methuen in London in 1891. Members of the colleges wrote the chapters on their own houses. The writers kept their own spelling and style, and no one forced a single mould on the set. A preface sets out the plan of the whole.

Clark argues that the history of one old college is more than enough for a volume. Each has seen great changes in its rules and has mirrored the state of the nation. Yet by letting each chapter stress what others omit, one volume can show both each college and college life at large across the ages.
5261-constance-dunlap:
Arthur B. Reeve's Constance Dunlap, in the Craig Kennedy series, follows a woman drawn into crime by her husband's troubles. Chapters run through forgers, embezzlers, gun runners, gamblers, eavesdroppers, clairvoyants, plungers, abductors, shoplifters, blackmailers, dope fiends, and fugitives, as Constance learns the underworld from the inside.

The book opens with Carlton Dunlap coming home late, hunted and desperate, and Constance must decide how far to follow him. Reeve gives his heroine unusual agency for a detective tale of the period, and the novel offers a fast tour of early twentieth-century crime, with Kennedy's science in the background.
52754-profits-from-scrap:
Profits from Scrap is a trade manual from the American Bureau of Engineering of Chicago, issued in 1922. The Bureau ran four arms: consulting engineers, a publishing house, a shop equipment business, and an electrical school. Its books served the electrical side of the auto trade. This one teaches shops to make money from waste.

The text works at bench level. Every battery that has to be opened, it says, must have its top connectors drilled off. That makes a heap of lead chips. The drillings have to be cleaned off and dealt with as value, not dirt. Around that core the manual builds a system for the battery and electrical service station: salvage, sorting, and sale. It is a plain specimen of the auto age's thrift literature.
54813-azalea-at-sunset-gap:
Elia Peattie wrote this girls' novel for her Blue Ridge series, set in the mountain country she made her own. Reilly and Britton of Chicago published it in nineteen fourteen, with art by Joseph Pierre Nuyttens. Azalea, a winsome mountain lass, had won friends in an earlier book of the set.

At Sunset Gap she meets new folk: riders bound for Bee Tree, a small lost brother, and a hall called Rowantree. Chapters promise war, a rescue told in two parts, a hermit thrush, and a rebel. Peattie's tales were praised as clean and wholesome, yet full of life. Girl readers of nine to ninety, as one notice said, found a friend in Azalea and her hills.
56402-brazil-the-river-plate-and-the-fal:
Brazil, the River Plate, and the Falkland Islands is a travel and commercial survey by William Hadfield, printed at London in 1854. Hadfield had been many years resident in Brazil and was secretary to the South American and General Steam Navigation Company. The book also covers the Cape Horn route to Australia. It adds notices of Lisbon, Madeira, the Canaries, and the Cape Verde islands.

The illustrations come, by permission, from the South American sketches of Sir W Gore Ouseley, late minister to the states of La Plata. Others are from the drawings of Sir Charles Hotham during his recent mission to Paraguay. Much new information is supplied on Paraguay and on the region of the Amazon. Portraits, maps, charts, and plans go with the text. A portrait of Don Pedro the Second, emperor of Brazil, fronts the volume.
58119-the-destruction-of-the-greek-empir:
The Destruction of the Greek Empire is a history by Edwin Pears, published in 1903. Longmans, Green issued it at London, New York, and Bombay. Its subtitle gives the story of the capture of Constantinople by the Turks. Maps and illustrations support the text. Pears had written The Fall of Constantinople, on the Fourth Crusade. He held Greek and Bulgarian orders, the title page notes. A preface discusses the authorities behind the narrative.

Pears lived in Constantinople and lacked the great libraries of Western Europe, he pleads. His Phrantzes comes from the Bonn series of Byzantine authors. Pachymer, Cantacuzenus, and Ducas he quotes from the Venetian edition. Archbishop Leonard's account he takes from another collection. He warns that his sources' battle numbers can rarely be trusted. Victims slaughtered or captured swell beyond any control, he admits.
59034-the-big-leap:
The Big Leap is a science fiction story by Charles Fritch, taken from Worlds of If Science Fiction of February 1955. Its headnote plays with the old slanders: the moon is green cheese and the stars are eyes, and we are all fleas on a big space animal. Do not let it worry you, it says, unless you take the first trip out into space, all alone. The hero, Cantrell, is taking that trip.

Tomorrow he would go so high and fast he would not come down again. It would be a shame to leave Earth, with her firmness and no great space underfoot. Then shame swept the cold feeling aside: fear of the unknown again. The psychologists could not erase that icy prickling.
59991-sermons-by-the-fathers-of-the-cong:
Volume six of Sermons by the Fathers of the Congregation of St Paul the Apostle was published in New York in 1871. The congregation, known as the Paulist Fathers, was founded by Isaac Hecker, who entered this volume for copyright. The preface says that strong sales of the earlier volumes, and requests from clergy at home and abroad, brought this one out.

Contents open with a sermon on the remembrance of mercies, from a text in Isaiah. A second treats the three gifts of the Magi: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The sermons were preached at St Paul's church on Fifty-ninth Street in New York. Printed sermons of this kind served priests seeking models and lay readers seeking teaching, and the Paulists used print as a main tool of their mission to America.
62068-the-face-of-the-earth-as-seen-from:
The Face of the Earth as Seen from the Air studies the application of airplane photography to geography. Its author, Willis Lee, worked for the Geological Survey. The book was published in New York in 1922. The book is special publication number 4 of the American Geographical Society. A front view looks obliquely down on the Capitol at Washington, with the Library of Congress behind.

Twelve chapters run from The Viewpoint through marshes and drainage, coastal mud flats, and drowned land forms, to mapping and charting from the air. Symbols mark each plate as an oblique or a vertical photograph. Lee argues that the airplane gives geography a new eye: patterns of plain, coast, and mountain read clearly from above. The book is an early manual of air survey, written when the method was new.
63295-the-wishing-cap:
The Wishing-Cap is a tale for the young by Mrs Sherwood. Sherwood was known for a famed tale of a small boy and his bearer. A fresh print of this tale came out at London from a press of church books. The tale opens with a rich lady of that town who had great wealth but had not given her heart to God.

She has the care of five young ones, four kin and one lone boy whose kin died past months past. That boy reads his gift book each day and tries to heed its good words. One feast day the lady joins the young at tea and vows to put on a wish cap. The young burn to see what fine things the cap will bring.
63818-a-half-century-among-the-siamese-a:
A Half Century Among the Siamese and the Lao is the life story of Daniel McGilvary, printed in 1912. McGilvary was a church worker who spent fifty years in Siam and among the Lao people. Arthur J Brown wrote a warm note of praise at the front.

Brown says he urged McGilvary, then past seventy five, to write his life while he still could. The book is given to McGilvary wife, and it holds many plates. McGilvary tells of his call, his trip out, and long years of work far from home. He writes as a man of faith who knew the land and its folk at close hand. Readers get a rare first hand tale of old Siam from a man who gave his life to it.
63838-time-trap:
Frank Belknap Long wrote Time Trap, a short tale that ran in a pulp magazine in the winter of 1948. Old Charley Grimes is the kind of man who has been all over the solar system. Around a campfire in the Rockies, his friends swap yarns to get him started on the dark side of the moon.

Charley tells of plodding across a dark crater on Luna, where someone waited for him who could not exist. The frame tale sets camp talk of the past against stark scenes of craters and thin light from a rocket's view pane. Long mixes tall-tale charm with dread: what Charley met out there still shapes the story he tells by the fire.
64585-the-trap:
The Trap, by Dorothy Richardson, is a novel in her Pilgrimage series. Duckworth issued it at London, first published in 1925, dedicated to Bryher. Pointed Roofs, Backwater, Honeycomb, and The Tunnel precede it in the series list. Miriam enters a short old London by street in chapter one here.

Rain washed flagstones gleam in the sequestered lane near Saint Pancras church spire. A blistered door bears her number, its knocker a worn iron face. Stone blocks and an alabaster finger fill the shop window beside it. A one eyed grey cat curls among the dusty marble scraps within. Stream of consciousness prose renders Miriam London life from inside.
66178-the-making-of-modern-japan-an-acco:
J H Gubbins, first secretary of the British embassy at Tokyo, wrote an account of Japan's progress, priced at twenty one shillings. It runs from pre feudal days to constitutional government and great power rank. Gubbins had compiled a dictionary of Chinese Japanese words. He had also translated the civil code of Japan. His earlier Progress of Japan covered 1853 to 1871. Chapters treat religion, the family system, and education.

The advertisement pages present the book among new titles on Asia. Gubbins wrote from inside the Tokyo embassy during Japan's transformation. His account explains Japanese institutions to British readers. The family system chapter reflects his legal work. The book is a diplomat's synthesis of Meiji change.
66183-man-trap:
Man-Trap is a science fiction story by Hal Annas, taken from Imagination magazine for December 1953. Jerry Kerran had vowed that no woman would ever entice him into matrimony. That was before Professor Madigan's invention: a new kind of magnetism, more powerful than gravity, working as a supplement to natural magnetism, and able to be controlled.

Jerry watches the announcement on his screen, where a woman addresses the girls of the audience directly. He switches off the current and growls at women in general. He has three rules: if she will not stay home, get rid of her. If she will stay, suspect her of matrimonial intentions and get rid of her too. Best of all, do not monkey with her to begin with. Rising to his lanky six feet, he opens his door and finds a girl there.
69777-the-rat-trap:
The Rat-Trap, a novel by Dolf Wyllarde, was copyrighted in 1904 and issued in New York in 1914. Wyllarde dedicates the book to the general public, the only critic whose opinion is finally worth having. A cast list names the staff of Key Island: Evelyn Gregory, its administrator and colonial secretary, and Alfred Halton, sent to probe recent riots.

Officers, wardens, a consul, a chaplain, a sugar planter, and officers' wives fill out the colonial world of Port Albert and China Town. The island had been run by the British African Island Company before the riots. Chapter one opens with a proverb warning against the man who talks under his breath, as a troop ship arrives. Power, race, and scandal simmer in Wyllarde's tale.
70921-the-little-cap:
Little Cap, or The Lost Heir of Sternfelden, is a tale by Mrs Dundas, printed at London. Its contents promise a call to battle, a birthday gift, and adversity for its folk. Gaspard and his family leave their home in the fourth chapter of the story. A christening follows, and the little cap of the title does its work.

The tale opens in 1552 with the siege of Metz by Emperor Charles the Fifth. French troops had just seized that strong town and its famed cathedral. The emperor tried in vain to win the place back from its defenders. Against that war ground a soldier family tale of loss and return unfolds.
71186-the-magazine-of-history-with-notes:
The Magazine of History with Notes and Queries, volume one, number four, is a monthly magazine dated April 1905, published by William Abbatt at New York. It sold for fifty cents a number, five dollars a year. The frontispiece shows the fountain at Lexington with the statue of the Minute Man. The contents open with a paper on the progress of discovery of the Mississippi River.

Warren Upham's first paper traces the river's discovery and mapping at its mouth to a voyage of Pinzon and Solis, with Amerigo Vespucci as astronomer and cartographer. Other pieces treat Confederate finance in Alabama, early legislative turmoils in New Jersey, and a hitherto unpublished poem of Edgar Allan Poe. A poem manuscript by Walt Whitman, The Patrol at Barnegat, is printed. Original documents include letters from Benjamin Hawkins and Silas Deane. Sections of minor topics and genealogy close the number.
72983-mabel-s-mishap:
Mabel's Mishap is a children's story by Amy Blanchard, published at Philadelphia in 1900. Blanchard also wrote A Dear Little Girl and Kittyboy's Christmas. Seven chapters tell the tale. A picture shows two children with little Louie playing in the laundry. The story opens on a dismal rainy day.

Mabel leans on the broad window-sill, watching drops trickle down the panes. Her paper dolls in gay tissue dresses sit in state before her. She has cut a whole company of flat-headed creatures from one piece of newspaper. Tired of them, she sweeps the lot onto the floor. The mishap of the title grows out of such a dull day indoors.
73243-the-trap:
The Trap, a tale by Henry Whitehead, ran in Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror in March 1932. The narrator teaches at a private school in Connecticut. His friend Browne runs the school. An old Copenhagen mirror hangs in his rooms there. He found it, dusty and cobwebbed, in an empty estate house in Santa Cruz. Its gilt frame was smashed and later repaired.

One December morning he thinks he sees motion in the glass. He sits alone, so he calls it an illusion. Yet a second mirror across the hall makes an endless corridor of reflections. Something seems to stir down that corridor. The head note says a subtle evil lurks in Canevin's mirror. Dread builds from one small, doubted sight.
75094-the-trap:
The Trap, a crime tale by Murray Leinster, opens with a cold promise: Colby's murder plan was perfect, except at one point. A head note calls the story instructive. It deals, the note says, with the value of a reputation and the best way to commit murder. Embarrassing letters and stolen thousand-dollar bills get their due as well.

Colby has thought about reputations with care. Yet the shot that kills Grahame is barely done echoing before he recalls the reputation of Detective Sergeant Nesbit. Cold sweat breaks on his forehead, and a sick feeling takes him. Grahame fell as planned, arms flung out, in the leaf-strewn mud among the trees. Leinster hangs the whole tale on that one flaw: the man waiting to read the scene.
77659-grandma-s-lie-soap:
Robert Abernathy wrote Grandma's Lie Soap, a tale with a grin in its frame. Grandma's soap, the blurb says, was a miracle of miracles under the stars. If you don't believe it, just try lying to the flying saucer folk. Of course you'll believe this story, the teller opens; everybody will. The funny thing is that it could be a lie.

His scene is a gathering of literary amateurs, where tame talk of Proust and Faulkner drives him to tell the tale. A frail old woman, a country lane, and a cake of home-made soap stand at its heart, with truth itself as the stakes. Fans get a sly tale of the saucer age.
77737-the-rat-trap:
The Rat Trap is a novel of intrigue by William Le Queux, issued at New York in 1930. Its contents are bare chapter numbers, running to twenty four without a single title. The tale opens in the marble hall of a gay hotel at Ostend. That town, the narrator says, is a reckless centre of bathing, gambling, and dancing. Two Englishmen stood chatting together in the hall.

The younger of the pair, about twenty two and dressed in tennis clothes, is cut off at the head of this copy as he is introduced. Le Queux wrote tale after tale of spies, secrets, and foreign plots, and Ostend in season was his natural ground. Englishmen abroad, a resort of pleasure, and danger under the polish: the rat trap of the title waits to spring.
9151-ruggles-of-red-gap:
Harry Leon Wilson wrote this comic novel in 1915 about Ruggles, an English valet lost in the American West. The tale opens in Paris, where Ruggles tends the Honourable George with exact care for collars, waistcoats, and beards. A lost wager soon sends him to Red Gap, a wild town in Washington state.

There Ruggles must learn American ways, from slang to saloons to self-reliance. Wilson mines the clash of English form and western freedom for laughs. Yet the comedy has heart, as Ruggles finds dignity in a new life. The novel remains a beloved classic of American humor.
britannica-1911-delaware-water-gap:
Delaware Water Gap is a borough and summer resort in Pennsylvania, set on the Delaware river north of Philadelphia. Rail lines on both banks serve it, and a tram line links it to a town a few miles west. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its counts at two census dates, a few hundred souls in each.

The borough takes its name from the gorge near by, famed for its fine views. In winter ice stacks in the river to a great height. Here the river cuts through a long ridge to its very base. Two mounts face each other across the gap, one in each state. The gap runs for about two miles through the range, and the rise of the river at that point is low next to the peaks.
britannica-1911-foolscap:
Foolscap is first the cap worn by jesters and fools: a conical hat with a cockscomb running up the centre of the back and bells attached. Dunces were made to wear a like conical cap. The name then passes to paper. Foolscap is a size of writing or printing paper, varying from 12 by 15 inches to 17 by 13 and a half inches. The paper took its name from a watermark, a fool's cap in the sheet.

A German example of that watermark from 1479 was shown at the Caxton Exhibition of 1877. The entry clears away two familiar tales. There is no trustworthy proof that Sir John Spielmann brought the mark to his Dartford mill in 1580. Nor is it true that the Rump Parliament swapped the royal arms for a fool's cap on the paper of its journals. The short article joins costume, paper sizes and a debunked legend.
britannica-1911-gap:
Gap, capital of the French department of the Hautes Alpes, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town held 6888 people in 1906, and its commune 10823. It is built at a height of 2418 feet on the right bank of the Luye. Snowy peaks far off to the north east crown the view.

The little city wears the white look of a Provençal town. Its cathedral church from the seventeenth century was rebuilt in full from 1866 to 1905. In the prefecture rests the tomb of the constable de Lesdiguières, from about 1613. The same house holds rich archives and sets of old finds and science goods. A few small works of local weight round out its trade. Rail lines join Gap to Briançon, Grenoble, and Marseilles.
britannica-1911-venus-s-fly-trap:
Venus's fly-trap, a plant that catches and eats insects, is the subject of this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. The plant is native to North and South Carolina. It was first described in 1768 by the American botanist Ellis, in a letter to Linnaeus. Ellis gave a sound account of its leaves and guessed that it fed on insects. Linnaeus called it a wonder of nature but thought the insects escaped.

Later work, above all by Charles Darwin in his book on such plants, proved the plant does feed on its prey. The article describes a small herb with a rosette of leaves. Each leaf has two lobes edged with spikes. The upper face bears tiny glands and three fine bristles set in a triangle. When an insect touches the bristles, the lobes close.
capitola-the-madcap:
Mrs. Emma D. E. N. Southworth, a popular American storyteller, continued her hit The Hidden Hand in Capitola the Madcap, as Part Two. Capitola Black, called Cap, is an orphan girl raised in Virginia hills. Her guardian, Major Warfield, known as Old Hurricane, storms through scene after scene. Villainy circles the Hidden House and its captive.

Chapters send Cap into the Hidden Hollow to free a prisoner held in the house. Black Donald, the outlaw chief, matches wits with her across disguises and pursuits. A court-martial, a verdict, and the end of a border war widen the plot beyond Virginia. Clara Day's fate, Traverse Rocke's errand, and Colonel Le Noir's schemes weave through Cap's adventures. A mysterious maniac's story unlocks secrets near the close. Southworth ends with prospects brightening and Capitola turned capitalist, in her own coin. Dime-novel energy, cross-dressing escapes, and cliffhangers made Cap a heroine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gap:
Gap, a diocese in the Hautes-Alpes of France, was suppressed in 1801, joined to Digne, and restored in 1822 with much of old Embrun added. Its first bishop, by liturgical tradition, was Saint Demetrius, disciple of the apostles, though Duchesne counts Constantinus, seen at Epaone in 517, as the first bishop history can prove. The entry weighs legend against record throughout.

Gap's bishops include Aregius, who built a famed literary school prized by Gregory the Great, and Arnoux, set over a simoniac predecessor. Embrun's long roll runs from Marcellinus in the fourth century through Henry of Segusio, the canonist called Ostiensis. It reaches Jacques Gelu, an early believer in Joan of Arc, and Giulio de' Medici, later Clement VII. Tournon's college crowns the tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walter-map:
Walter Map, sometimes wrongly written Maps, was Archdeacon of Oxford, born at or near Hereford about 1140 and dying between 1208 and 1210. Probably Welsh by extraction from the Marches, he became known through medieval church Latin and the Norman French of Henry II's court and law courts. At fourteen he went to Paris university, studying until 1160 under Girard la Pucelle, and by 1162 he was at England's court.

Henry made him a clerk of his household, implying he had taken or was about to take holy orders. Preferments followed: king's representative at the Third Lateran Council in 1179, where he disputed with the Waldensians, various benefices, and finally the Oxford archdeaconry in 1197. A failed bid for Hereford brought him into contact with St Hugh of Lincoln.
constance-dunlap:
Arthur B. Reeve's Constance Dunlap belongs to his Craig Kennedy series, though Kennedy stays offstage. Carlton Dunlap comes home late with the look of a hunted animal. His wife Constance, awake behind feigned sleep, hears his confession. He has forged, and the law is closing in.

Constance takes up crime to shield the husband she loves. The Forgers, The Embezzlers, The Gun Runners, and The Gamblers title her cases. She outwits detectives, fleeces plungers, and joins the criminals she studies. Reeve reverses his usual formula: the woman at the centre is the outlaw, not the scientist. Each episode is a complete caper with its own underworld trade explained. The book is a sympathetic portrait of a lady crook, written when that was a scandalous novelty. Constance's loyalty, not her loot, is the point Reeve keeps making.
doe-osti-17136604-2026-r-matrix-workshop:
Marco Pigni and a large multi lab group record the 2026 R-Matrix Workshop on neutron induced reactions, in report ORNL/TM-2026/4816 dated September 2026. R matrix theory is the standard frame for fitting neutron reaction data into evaluated nuclear data files. The workshop gathered evaluators to compare methods, codes, and problem cases.

Opening lectures cover theory from the Green Bloch view, experimental methods, and recent evaluations for nitrogen and copper isotopes. Five days of question and answer sessions follow, one per talk. Topics range from automated fitting and SAMMY code modernization to uncertainty work with SCALE and transmission measurements. Talks also treat carbon breakup channels, thermal neutron scattering, and fluorine data validation, with editorial notes closing each day.
doe-osti-17197395-2026-r-matrix-workshop: The R-matrix workshop's 2026 methods got their proceedings again, and this report covers neutron-induced reactions. The pages record the talks. The theorists get their notes. The year was 2026. The notes were theoretical. The talks were recorded. The reactions were neutron-induced.
doe-osti-2589588-opportunities-in-ai-for:
Where artificial intelligence could serve the electric grid is mapped in Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11809, by Logan Blakely, Matthew Reno, Scott Steinmetz, and co-authors. Grid work is high-stakes: a wrong model output can mislead operators who keep power flowing. The report weighs new AI tools against that risk, section by section.

Topics include human factors, uncertainty measurement, and methods that explain why a model reached its answer. One chapter covers judging whether an AI system is trustworthy enough for high-consequence use. Sandia's own analysis platforms, Dakota and the Uncertainty Quantification Toolkit, appear as in-house strengths built since 1993. The survey gives grid researchers a shared agenda: adopt AI where it helps, with proof it behaves under stress.
doe-osti-3022935-watching-for-light-an-e:
John H Ganter of Sandia National Laboratories lays out an enterprise roadmap for laser threat warning, the job of spotting laser threats against space assets. Report SAND2026-18159R argues that warning gear alone is not enough. A system earns trust only when it catches real events and also resists false alarms, and outside the lab even the roles lasers play can be unclear.

Ganter builds his plan like an industry model for an enterprise that produces trustworthy warnings as a routine product. Psychology and economics enter the design, since distracted partners with different goals must be given reasons to share what they know. Worked scenes show analysts passing evidence needs along within a minute while commanders press for answers.
doe-osti-3028691-measurement-of-the-qe-m:
Igor Pinayev of Brookhaven National Laboratory documents a quantum efficiency mapping procedure in technical note BNL-229637-2026-TECH, dated April 2026. Quantum efficiency says how many electrons a photocathode emits per incoming photon, and it varies across the cathode surface. A QE map scans a laser spot over the surface in a grid, (2N+1) squared points in the scheme described, and records the response at each stop.

Calibration comes first. A mirror swings in to send the laser, running continuous-wave at 78 kilohertz pulse rate, onto a power meter. Pulse energy follows from the average power, and photons per pulse from the photon energy, 2.39 electron volts here. The scan then assumes that pulse energy holds steady while the mirror retracts and the spot walks its grid, a stated assumption the note flags for the operator.
doe-osti-3101845-subsurface-mafic-and-ul:
Estibalitz Ukar of the University of Texas at Austin led the SubMAP-CO2 project under grant DE-FE0032249, running from July 2023 with an extension through December 2025. Peter B. Kelemen, Shuvajit Bhattacharya, and D. Nicolas Espinoza shared leadership. The project mapped mafic and ultramafic rocks buried across the United States. These dark, magnesium-rich rocks react with carbon dioxide and lock it into solid carbonate minerals, a storage form that cannot leak back as gas.

Surface outcrops of such rock are well studied, but the buried resource had never been sized at national scale. The team paired mapping with lab carbonation tests on real samples, then posted results in a web portal called GeoMAFIC. Layers show uptake math for each mineral phase, under full or half capture of the peak dissolved magnesium.
doe-osti-3363379-large-power-transformer:
Vignesh Ramasamy, Aubryn Cooperman, Rakesh Jayswal, and Margaux Seward of the National Laboratory of the Rockies extend their earlier gap analysis in this supplemental report. It covers the large power transformer supply chain (NLR/TP-5700-96742, May 2026). These transformers serve as the generator step-up units that connect hydropower plants to the transmission grid, so rehabilitation projects stall without them.

The supplement digs into delivered cost and domestic content strategy. Moving an imported unit can add hundreds of thousands of dollars in shipping, port handling, route surveys, and permits. Regions with existing manufacturing and assembly capacity gain shorter lead times and lower logistical risk. Cost estimates rest on a figure near $15 per kilowatt, escalated from a 2014 federal study.
doe-osti-3365144-omega-the-ocean-model-f:
A Los Alamos National Laboratory highlight sheet, LA-UR-26-24115, dated May 8, 2026, introduces Omega, the new ocean model for the E3SM Earth system model. Mark Petersen, Luke Van Roekel, and Steven Brus wrote it. Omega version 0 is rebuilt from the ground up in C++ with the Kokkos library, so the same code runs fast on both ordinary processors and graphics processors. It replaces the aging MPAS-Ocean model.

Benchmarks on three supercomputers show the payoff. On Frontier, Omega's combined CPU and GPU run took 0.18 seconds against 8.5 seconds for the older model on the same test, with good scaling as more nodes were added. Version 0 solves the shallow water equations with passive tracers, the first step toward a full ocean circulation model. Faster oceans open higher-resolution climate simulations.
doe-osti-3391006-example-alternative-com:
The Example Alternative Compliance Waiver Application is a July 2026 guidance document in the EPAct State and Alternative Fuel Provider Fleet Program. It shows a covered fleet how to ask the Department of Energy for a waiver. The waiver lets it meet petroleum reduction goals instead of buying alternative fuel vehicles. The department provides a planning spreadsheet for the purpose. The example includes every component a complete application must contain.

The sample applicant is Example Fleet, ID number 1255, applying for model year 2028. Its average light-duty fuel use is estimated at 650 gasoline gallon equivalents per vehicle per year. That figure is drawn from fleet data for 2002 through 2004. The covered inventory is 75 vehicles. The petroleum reduction requirement is therefore 48,750 gasoline gallon equivalents. The application package adds the reduction plan itself. It also adds a certification of compliance with vehicle emissions standards.
doe-osti-3452085-myriad-world-baseline-g:
Oak Ridge technical report dated June 2026 builds Myriad World Baseline, a set of global population estimates by place, age, and sex. Joseph V. Tuccillo, James D. Gaboardi, Andrew Zimmer, Alexandre Sorokine, and Marie L. Urban wrote the report. Planners use such baselines for health, aid, and risk work.

The method joins cohort labels for age and gender by LandScan grid cell. Change factors then shift estimates to a target year. Results are written to a compressed parquet file for sharing. Element-wise math keeps the update fast across millions of cells. Users get a current world population surface from checked source data.
madcap:
Madcap is a romantic adventure novel by George Gibbs. Its heroine is Hermia, and the first picture shows her teasing Mr. Markham. She tells him he must flirt and make pretty speeches. Chapters promise a gorilla, a marooning, and a rescue.

Olga Tcherny and the Fabiani family widen the plot's circle. There are mountebanks, a fairy godmother, and vagabond days. Danger comes, and with it a lady in the dark. Gibbs piles incident on incident in the old romantic manner. Hermia's madcap spirit drives every scene she enters. The book is light, swift, and full of improbable fun.
obed-hussey-who-of-all-inventors-made-br:
Follett L. Greeno edited Obed Hussey, Who, of All Inventors, Made Bread Cheap in 1912. Greeno calls it a true record of Hussey's life and struggles to introduce the reaper. Pamphlets by Hussey's friends and associates are reprinted here, with added facts and testimonials. Pictures show Hussey's American reaper and the inventor himself.

Hussey, of Quaker stock, was born in Maine in 1792 and moved early to Nantucket. Like other Nantucket boys he went whaling in his youth. Quiet and studious, he had a strong bent for intricate machines. He worked as a skillful draftsman at inventions all his life. A steam plow and a corn and cob mill stand among them.
ruggles-of-red-gap:
Harry Leon Wilson wrote Ruggles of Red Gap, dated 1915 and given to Helen Cooke Wilson. A front picture carries the line, I take it you failed to win the hundred pounds, sir. Chapter One opens at 6:30 in a Paris apartment, where the narrator, a valet, has just finished dressing the Honourable George. He is pleased, on the whole, with his work. Those last touches, he holds, mark the gap between a man well turned out and a man merely dressed.

Pride in craft runs through the opening talk, down to collars, waistcoats, and beards. The Honourable George's dress waistcoats no longer let him take a full breath, and his collars clasp too closely. The valet holds that a collar can give ample room if its depth is at least two and one quarter inches.
somewhere-in-red-gap:
Harry Leon Wilson sets Somewhere in Red Gap at the Arrowhead ranch, with pictures by John R. Neill, F. R. Gruger, and Henry Raleigh. The book, given to George Horace Lorimer, came out at New York from Grosset and Dunlap. Contents heads promise the Red Splash of Romance, Ma Pettengill and the Song of Songs, real Peruvian doughnuts, Cousin Egbert stepping in, and a piece called Little Old New York.

Chapter I opens in the big living room of the ranch house. Its walls are decked here and there with the prizes of the owner, Mrs. Lysander John Pettengill. Among them hang family portraits in crayon and cuts of noble beasts clipped from the Breeder's Gazette. One cut shows her standing on the centre table to see herself in the glass over the mantel.
the-submarine-boys-and-the-middies-the-p: Victor G. Durham's third book of the Submarine Boys series, dated 1909, sends Jack Benson and his friends to Annapolis as a prize detail. Only the title page and the heading of chapter one appear in this record. A contents list of twenty-four chapters stands with them. The cruise itself does not appear. The titles promise varied episodes. Eph flirts with science in one. Two kinds of voodoo appear. The boys squint at the Camelroorelephant. Marines hold men up. A companion Saalfield record lists only twenty chapters.
the-voyage-of-the-rattletrap: Hayden Carruth published The Voyage of the Rattletrap with Harper and Brothers in New York in 1897, illustrated by H. M. Wilder. He dedicates the book to John Briar, a poor cook but a good fellow. The pages present here hold the title page, contents, and illustrations list, so the journey's narrative does not appear. Chapter headings trace a wagon route from Lookout Lake to the Missouri River, into Nebraska, and across the Niobrara. Later chapters cross the sand hills toward the Black Hills and Deadwood, then turn homeward bound.
the-world-war-and-what-was-behind-it-or-: L. P. Bénézet, a school superintendent in Evansville, Indiana, wrote The World War and What Was Behind It. A contents list of twenty-six chapters is present here, without the chapters themselves. His subtitle calls the book the story of the map of Europe. Chapters run from Rome and the barbarian tribes to the war's cost. Bismarck appears as the Man of Blood and Iron. A closing chapter asks what Germany must learn.
theory-of-silk-weaving-a-treatise-on-the: Arnold Wolfensberger, a graduate of the Textile Institute of Zurich, wrote a treatise on silk weaving published in New York in 1921. The second revised and enlarged edition contains ninety-five plates. Its subject is the construction and application of weaves for broad and narrow silk fabrics. Plain, novelty, and Jacquard fabrics all fall within its scope, along with decomposition and calculation of weaves. A heading for drawing-in appears on page five. The opening pages and title matter are what is present here, so Wolfensberger's instructions themselves are not shown.
